fields.h1: George Müller and the God Who Answers Prayer
fields.meta_title: George Müller and the God Who Answers Prayer
fields.description: George Müller cared for thousands of orphans on prayer alone, never asking anyone but God for a penny. His life is a living proof that God still answers prayer.
fields.body_html:
George Müller cared for more than ten thousand orphans over his lifetime, built five large orphan houses, and supported missionaries and schools around the world — and through it all he never once asked a single human being for money. Instead, he asked God. Müller’s life stands as one of history’s great demonstrations that God hears and answers prayer, for over sixty years he ran his vast work on the simple principle of telling his needs to God alone and trusting him to provide. His story is a standing rebuke to unbelief and a mighty encouragement to every Christian who wonders whether God really answers when we pray. “And my God will supply every need of yours according to his riches in glory in Christ Jesus” (Philippians 4:19) — Müller set out to prove that promise true, and God honoured his faith again and again.

From wayward youth to man of God

Müller was born in Prussia in 1805 and spent his early years as a thief and a liar; by his own account he stole even from his own father, and was once jailed for running up debts he could not pay. He was studying for the ministry with no real faith when, at a small prayer meeting, he was converted and his life turned completely. The grace that reached down to such a young man became the theme of his life — proof that God can transform anyone.

Settling eventually in Bristol, England, Müller gave himself to the work of God among the poor. Moved by the plight of orphaned children who filled the streets and workhouses, he resolved to open a home for them. But he determined to do it in a way that would demonstrate to a doubting world that God is living and faithful — the whole enterprise would be sustained by prayer and faith alone, without appeals for funds or the backing of wealthy patrons.

A life built on prayer alone

This was the radical heart of Müller’s ministry. He would make his needs known to no one but God. When money ran short, he prayed; when food was needed for hundreds of children, he prayed; when a building was required, he prayed. And time after time, often at the very last moment, the provision came — an unexpected gift, a knock at the door, a sum that exactly met the need. Müller kept careful records of tens of thousands of specific answers to prayer, a documented testimony that God is not deaf.

One famous morning the orphans sat before empty plates with no food in the house; Müller thanked God for the breakfast he had not yet seen, and within minutes a baker who had felt unaccountably compelled to bake bread arrived, followed by a milkman whose cart had broken down outside. Such stories filled his life. He was living out Jesus’ promise: “If you then, who are evil, know how to give good gifts to your children, how much more will your Father who is in heaven give good things to those who ask him!” (Matthew 7:11). Müller took God at his word and found him faithful.

Why he did it this way

Müller was clear about his motive. He did not run his orphanages by faith merely because it was efficient or because he lacked other options; he did it deliberately, as a witness. He longed to strengthen the faith of God’s people and to show the unbelieving world that the God of the Bible is real and answers prayer today. His life was, in effect, a decades-long experiment designed to test and display the faithfulness of God — and the results were overwhelming.

He rooted his confidence in the promises of Scripture, which he searched daily and pleaded back to God. He clung to words like “those who seek the Lord lack no good thing” (Psalm 34:10) and “seek first the kingdom of God and his righteousness, and all these things will be added to you” (Matthew 6:33). And he insisted that such faith was not a special gift given only to him, but the birthright of every believer who would take God at his word. “Without faith it is impossible to please him, for whoever would draw near to God must believe that he exists and that he rewards those who seek him” (Hebrews 11:6) — Müller believed it, and acted on it, and God rewarded that faith before a watching world.

The secret behind the miracles

The real secret of Müller’s life was not a technique but a relationship. He began each day by getting his own heart happy in God before he did anything else, feeding his soul on Scripture until his faith was strong. He aimed, he said, to have his soul at peace with God first, so that everything else flowed from communion rather than anxiety. His prayers were not attempts to twist God’s arm but the requests of a child who knew his Father’s heart.

He also prayed according to God’s will and for God’s glory, confident in the promise: “this is the confidence that we have toward him, that if we ask anything according to his will he hears us” (1 John 5:14). Müller’s faith was not presumption; it was trust in a God he knew to be good, generous, and true to his word. “Every good gift and every perfect gift is from above, coming down from the Father of lights” (James 1:17), and Müller spent his life receiving such gifts and giving God the glory for every one.

More than orphans

Though the orphan houses were his most famous work, Müller’s ministry ranged far wider, and all of it ran on the same principle of believing prayer. Through the institution he founded, he supported the distribution of many thousands of Bibles and Christian books, funded schools that educated tens of thousands of children, and helped support missionaries labouring in distant lands — including, for a time, some of the pioneers of the modern missionary movement. The streams of provision that flowed in answer to his prayers watered far more than the orphanages he is remembered for.

Remarkably, in his seventies — an age when most men retire — Müller embarked on a new career as a travelling preacher, journeying some two hundred thousand miles across dozens of countries to tell of the God who answers prayer and to call believers to deeper faith. He kept at it into his ninetieth year. To the very end he lived by the same rule, trusting God for each day’s needs and finding him faithful, and he gave away almost all the money that passed through his hands, dying a poor man who had handled fortunes for God.

What Müller’s life teaches us

Müller’s example calls every believer to a bolder confidence in prayer. Most of us pray small, timid prayers because our view of God is small; Müller prayed vast prayers because he knew a vast and faithful God. His life urges us to bring our real needs to God, to expect him to answer, and to trust him when the answer tarries — for God’s timing is part of his faithfulness, and he often waits until the last moment to display his power the more clearly.

His life also teaches that faith and diligence go together. Müller prayed as if everything depended on God and worked as if much depended on him too — keeping meticulous accounts, caring for the children with excellence, and ordering the whole work wisely. Faith did not make him idle; it made him fearless. “No good thing does he withhold from those who walk uprightly” (Psalm 84:11), and Müller proved it across a long and fruitful life.

His enduring witness

George Müller died in 1898, having seen God supply, over his lifetime, sums equivalent to many millions in today’s money — all in answer to prayer, all without a single appeal to man. He left little for himself, having given away nearly everything, but he left the church an incomparable legacy: living proof that God still hears and answers the prayers of his children.

His story invites us to ask: what might God do through a life wholly given to prayer and trust? Müller was not a superhuman saint but an ordinary, once-wayward man who simply believed God’s promises and acted on them. The same God he trusted is our God still, and the same promises hold. Jesus’ invitation stands over every reader: “Ask, and it will be given to you; seek, and you will find; knock, and it will be opened to you” (Luke 11:9). George Müller took that invitation at face value — and so may we. His life leaves us with a searching question and a great encouragement in the same breath: if God did all this for one ordinary man who simply believed him, what might he yet do for a church, or a Christian, willing to trust him as fully? The answer is written across Müller’s ninety-two years in ten thousand answered prayers — and the God who wrote it has not changed.
